abstract: Ionizing radiation causes DNA double-strand breaks and disrupts chromatin architecture, potentially leading to chromosomal aberrations and genomic instability. Chromosome conformation capture (3C) technologies, particularly Hi-C, have revolutionized our understanding of three-dimensional genome organization. Here we review the intersection of radiation biology with chromatin conformation studies, examining how radiation impacts nuclear organization at multiple scales from nucleosomes to chromoso

methods.name: Review of cell-kill models (target theory, LQ, dual radiation action)
methods.description: Surveys Lea's target theory, Chadwick-Leenhouts molecular theory, and Kellerer-Rossi dual radiation action as frameworks for radiation-induced lethal lesions.
methods.evidence: the ‘Molecular the- ory’ of Chadwick and Leenhouts and the ‘Theory of Dual Radiation Action’ described by Kellerer and Rossi have been described

methods.name: Synthesis of Hi-C / chromosome conformation capture proximity data
methods.description: Interprets published genome-wide 3C/Hi-C contact data to relate chromatin spatial organization to formation of radiation-induced rearrangements.
methods.evidence: These techniques assay the spatial struc- ture of the nuclear chromatin at a whole-genome scale, a tool of particular relevance to radiation-induced aberrations.

methods.name: Cross-reading Hi-C contacts with transcription and translocation data
methods.description: Draws on studies linking Hi-C compartments to transcriptional activity and to clinically relevant translocation partner proximity.
methods.evidence: the Hi-C contact database generated by Lieberman-Aiden was cross- referenced with a large set of clinically relevant translocations

key_findings: The review describes the linear DNA strand over several Mbp as a fractal globule whose multiple contact sites may facilitate deletions or inversions if damaged.
Transcriptionally active euchromatin occupies a distinct space and is preferentially susceptible to free radical attack, which may favor rearrangements within that compartment.
The authors argue that the contribution of DNA repair programs to radiation lethality may depend on the spatial organization of the breaks, not just rejoining ability.
They propose that, if pre-irradiation chromatin state biases rejoining, transcriptome-modulating tools (e.g. RNAi, microRNA) could be an unexplored route to radiosensitization.
The review concludes that answering its open questions will likely require single-cell Hi-C merged with aberration analysis in irradiated material.
